transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Radai.
I'm your host, Eddie Palmigan, and today we're excited to have Klaus Kleinfeldt on the show.
Klaus is a seasoned business leader whose career includes 20 years at Siemens,
where he first headed the company's largest region, the US, before he in 2005 became Siemens's global CEO.
Klaus has also been 10 years at the helm of the New York-based aluminum company, Alkoa,
as well as an advisor to Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince.
In his book, Leading to Thrive, Kleinfeldt shares his lessons from leading organizations,
but also how to live a good life.
His book has received praise from a number of prominent people.
One of them is Steven Schwarzmann, this chairman, CEO, and co-founder of Blackstone,
who writes that Klaus's insights are both practical and inspiring, perfect for leaders at any stage.
Leading to Thrive was published in 2024, and we're excited to have his author on the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Klaus Kleinfeldt.
Hi Klaus, and welcome to Invest in By the Books podcast.
Hello Eddie, lovely to be with you.
Thank you for coming on, where are we reaching you?
I'm in my home office a little bit outside of New York City looking at the ocean that is
probably connecting us. Wow, and you have a lot of nice paintings in the background as well.
Yeah, it brings me energy. I love those.
And to begin for our listeners, I'm curious about your upbringing and how this has shaped you as a person.
It has influenced me greatly.
I was born in the north of Germany in Bremen, which once was occupied by Sweden,
but long, long time ago, all good, all good, you know, and had a good impact on the attic town.
So grew up with kind of the air of the sea and trade and investing.
So my parents, however, were refugees from East Germany.
They had fled, and my father started after coming back from the war, started his education.
All went very well. He became an aerospace engineer, but unfortunately he died when I was 10.
And then life took a twist. And my mother started going back to work.
I mean, number one, I was accelerated in my growing up, but my mother went to work.
And then she also decided in the vacation times that she didn't have time for me to send me back
to East Germany to spend time with my relatives. And that was the other thing.
I mean, one thing was the death of my father at a young age that influenced me greatly,
but the other thing that also influenced me greatly is having basically grown up.
In two systems, one being a free democracy, another one being a so-called socialistic
suppressive system, and seeing how people deal with that and learning the concept of freedom.
And it's one of those concepts that you only realize when it's taken away from you.
I noticed that in the conversations that I had in school back in school then when I got older,
whereas my colleagues didn't understand how much I was appreciating the aspects of a free
speech or a free choice of your own occupation, even education. And I'd seen all of this,
I mean, being not normal in the East. So those were two major things that influenced me.
And then around us, I mean, I think all of this, how about towns
have a way that you almost can't avoid to understand the world is large, and there are many,
many different cultures and many different norms. So that also probably has had a big influence
on me. That's a good point. But I'm curious also, what led you into the world of business,
and how was that journey? Well, what led me into the world of business was the pure need of making
money. I mean, it was pretty clear that money was tied. I was 10. I didn't know what to do,
but I had my first paying job at 12, you know, and was filling supermarket racks in the supermarket
that was close to us. And from then on, I have basically done gazillions, gazillions of different
jobs all the time. Never stopped working. Did you also have a natural way of doing this?
Was it something that came in aid for you? Oh, in the beginning, it doesn't come natural to you,
because you have to, you have to think of what value do you create. I mean, it's really,
I mean, because in the end you have to say, what value do I create to some people that they're
willing to pay me at 12? It's illegal to employ somebody, although I was employed. Fortunately,
I was a little bit taller and looked older, and the supermarket manager didn't realize how young I
was, or at least he didn't let me feel this. And he paid me in cash, you know, so that's the
other thing, you know, but no, it didn't come natural. But the fascination then set in
once I was in it. And I got fascinated by how what triggers certain businesses, how you can
make money, what different ways there are to make money. I was fascinated with what we
now call culture at that time. I mean, living it, looking at it from the bottom, and you see how
different leaders run it well or really scoot up and learning what you feel like one day when you
grow up, you hopefully want to do it, and then also learning what you definitely don't want to do,
but learning it with a view not from the top, with a view from the bottom. That I think has
even today wonderfully helps me to assess this, you know. And I think also the perspective of making
money, the concept of money was freedom to me, you know, it was, I mean, it allowed me to do things
that otherwise I wouldn't be able to do, so I was constantly looking for how can I increase the
value of whatever I can offer. And how has that changed over time, your perception of money?
Well, I mean, I always looked at what am I good at, you know, so for instance, one thing I did
already when I was young, I was always good at math, felt that that was easy for me, so I started
tutoring, you know, and even which I was resistant of tutoring some kids in my own age, you know,
as I thought this, I mean, I can't do that, but frankly, I mean, why not, I mean, if they come from
wealthy backgrounds and feel that I can help them and they relate to me, why not? So I've always
looked for that, then I did programming at an early age when I got my hands on a computer,
when I studied, actually, I chose my field of study because I wanted to have access to the
real computer, you know, and I wanted to be a programmer, which I did quite a while, then I became
a tutor, you know, at university, and that's, I mean, we're on, and the other way, the interesting
thing also is important. I never, I mean, I never was basically thinking, I have to be a CEO,
I want to be a boss of something, that was not, that was not what was driving me, what was
driving me, when I moved on, is that I felt I had a lot of people who were basically my bosses,
who I really didn't like, and where I, either I didn't like them, I didn't like the leadership
style, or I felt that they didn't make the best decisions and in spite of what knowledge they had
for either kind of own power reasons, political reasons, or just because they were not intelligent
enough to combine these things. So that was the thing that drove me, and I was shocked, I mean,
the more I move through the ranks, how far I had to go, to be honest, you know, to feel like,
oh, wow, this is the, I need to move on. And one of the things that, one mantra that I adopted early
was, love it, change it, or leave it, right? And I've basically lived by the principle all of my
life. And I think partially it was also because when you're confronted with the issue of death at
a very young age, you know, it makes you understand life is not forever. There is a beginning and
there is an end. So I somehow implicitly had this thought, hey, you have to use it in the best
possible way so that in the end, when the day comes, you know, that I feel I have led a fulfilled
life. And fittingly enough, we will speak about your book today, leaving to thrive. That's a good idea.
How did it come about this book? Well, look, I mean, if you would have asked me two years to go
close, would you ever write a book, I would have said no way because I'm sitting behind my computer
way too, way too many hours anyway, you know, so, but what happened is I had done a training program
as an active CEO, I mean, I had created a training program for a consulting company years ago
and they wrote it outward, what big success. And it was great. And then they came back to me and said,
can you do something even more effective? So I started this, this has been wrote out, it's very,
very effective. And I told them I want to do it, not just in a basic weekend format, but it's
not, it's a nine month format, basically, where, and I also told them I want to do it, not just talking
about the normal business things, we probably start with that because I don't know the individuals.
But to really change somebody, you have to understand what I call the in our game. You really have
to understand that. That was one pathway. The other pathway is I started to invest in companies that
are two to five years away from going public. And I shockingly saw that this aspect of burnout
existed extremely much. Also in this group of people who are, the leaders are probably around
their mid 30s, early to mid 30s, you know, and I had some very devastating experiences with
individuals, you know, that were the, I mean, almost died, you know, from from overwork and burnout
at that age. And I thought, wow, I mean, they clearly don't have a concept on how to read their
business life and also how to read their life because in a way, I mean, I always thought that
you only have one life. So in a way, you know, whatever you bring your energy to, whether you bring
it to business or whether you bring it to something else, I mean, it all comes back to the same core.
I mean, you got to get yourself in, you have to manage yourself, right? And that's what I
call the, you know, game. And then I, then I saw that the demand for this was so high that I
thought I have to codify that and I have to write it, write it in a book so that people who won't
get to know me, you know, at least have an access to this. So I've had, I have to provide this framework
that has done me well. And I've seen also how many leaders that I have been coaching
have hugely benefited from it. I would say, and I think they would also say that.
It's great that you have written this book and you have divided it into two main sections.
And the first one is, as you mentioned, the inner game and mastering that inner game. So what is
this? Well, the inner game is the question of how, how, how do you manage energy in the end?
I mean, many people I also included, I thought always it's all about managing time and being
effective. And as you know, I mean, I think the sweets are in a way a bit like the Germans,
it's all about discipline and all you prow through, you know. So, and that's the mantra that I use
until I realize that it's really not about time management, it's really about managing your
energy. And also, and because you get up in the morning, you feel usually relatively good and during
the course of the day, the energy burns through. So the question of what burns the energy,
and how do you replenish it? And I saw this analogy, interesting need to the high performance
sports. I mean, I love to play tennis. And I saw in the tennis world, the top player has got
longer in the top and state super fit, you know, and the average age went up in the top, you know.
Whereas in the business world, the opposite was happening. You know, the average tenure was going
down. People burned out earlier and I thought, wow, there's something to learn from these high
performance folks. And I looked at what they've done differently. And I realized this is the energy
concept. And so the question is, what is the sources of energy do you have? And it goes back to,
I mean, it goes back to body, mind and soul. I mean, there's these three levels of energy.
And then there's this aspect of purpose. And so on the body side, I mean, it's all about how
do you treat your body? What's the physical side of things? So do you move it? You know, what do you
eat? You stay hydrated? What do you? How much do you sleep? And those type of things, most of them
are well understood in some nascent ways. But then the other part, the mind part, I break it up into
emotional and mental. And that is not so well understood. I mean, I know that every one of us,
including myself, you know, have had moments when you say, oh, my God, I had this meeting. I got
really burned out. I got aggravated. I got so angry. And when you, even when you talk about that,
you wrap up and you feel the energy, your own energy is leaving you, right? So there are tricks
how to, so I commend that, you know, how to basically stay very cool in an environment and how to
let the energy not, let the trigger not trigger you to exert energy because people have to understand
the emotion is inside of you. So it's not like the emotion immediately gets, gets thrown on you,
you know, like it is physical. It is something that you have a choice. You allow whether this
emotion is going to get created and you are not. And you can train yourself. And that's what all
these high performance athletes are doing to not get triggered, you know, to end to fast recharge.
I mean, all these tennis players have a routine where in between, in between serves, they have
a trick where they rehearse a neurodengistic programming anchor so that a video goes on in their
mind when they turn around, get the new balls, you know, and then have the new serve. And in this
moment, when they have done this, you know, they feel like I'm new in the game. I've reset. I've
reset. So those are things that we can use in the business world, happy to talk about more.
On the mental side, it's really a question of what do you focus on? There's this great story of
the old shoemaker, you know, who has two sons. And he wants to give the business to one of the
sons and says, I want to test them and send them to Africa. One goes to the west coast, the other
to the east coast. One on the west coast sends a note back and says, oh, father, I'm very sorry to
tell you there's no market here. Everybody is barefoot. The other son, you know, sends a
note back, father, amazing. You send me as many shoes as you can get. This market is endless.
Everybody is barefoot. You know, and how many times have I seen that a great leaders have a way
to see things in a situation where the common wisdom is different. So, and I think a lot of people
train themselves, which is nice and early, early life to say, well, let me try to see multiple
elements. Particularly, I've seen this also in the investor world, the greatest investors look
at it and say, well, this is what I see in all of the reports, but what else do I see? Is there
something behind it? Are there some drivers there? And the really successful ones realize this
at a much earlier point in time, you know? So this is, I mean, this is on the on the mental and
emotional side, and then the spiritual side of things, you know, is something that rarely gets
talked about, but it is a super powerful thing. And many people think about meditation and self,
which is, which is very good. But at the same time, I mean, I think also the belief in something
greater than yourself is a thought that we should at least allow ourselves, you know? And I
think I would encourage people, for me, it has done amazing things in my life. I would, I would
say people try it out, you know, and see how well it works or works on you. And the last thing here
on this energy side is this aspect of purpose, which I've struggled with for a very long time and
used the book actually to clarify this for me. And purpose does to energy what a laser does to light.
Right, a laser when light is diffused, you know, laser comes in, boom, the focus is it, and it goes
through the big walls, you know, and heavy things, you know? And that's the same thing with purpose,
you know? So purpose and energy, you have a purpose, you will realize if you know what you're
here for, you will jump out of bed in the morning. And one of the other things that I noticed is
people think it's only one thing, but I don't think it's really only one thing. It is multiple things,
we have multiple roles, it's multiple purposes, you know? Very much that you think, oh, I would see
my girlfriend today. This makes me very, very happy, you know, all my, my group of friends, you know?
Or you'd say, I go to business and I will invent something new, work on something new, or I make sure
that a customer gets that delivery soon. This is stuff that should get you out of bed. That's a good
test for purpose. Can you give an example of when managing your energy has, has helped you as a leader?
Oh yeah, I mean, I've become obsessed with that and it's helped me greatly. I mean, for instance,
when you are in a negotiation and the negotiation goes on and obviously the other side is very
often very advanced and trying to basically run you down, you know, so that hopefully at the end
of the day, there's limited time for all of us that you feel under pressure to give in, you know?
And I think to be clear and make sure that you have to have basically a controller in your hat,
to say to say, okay, the other side is trying to provoke me, you know, with certain things or
with certain aspects. I'm not even going to take that in. I'm kind of let it go into this year,
come out of this year, you know? But I will stay focused on what I want to achieve and prepare my
arguments, you know? And then that's one, that's one defensive thing. One offensive thing is how
can you regain your energy and you can use this time, for instance, to concentrate on your own
breathing and just say, I have a breath going like a wave through my body. I breathe in. The other
side won't even notice this. I goes out, goes in, goes out, you know? On the mental side, another
really, really good trick is compartmentalization. I mean, a lot of people tell me, I have a hard
time to switch off when I'm at home and want to spend time with my family. And I've seen this,
unfortunately, way too often that people say, you know what? I had this lovely dinner at home with
the kids. But I still don't have a good relationship with them. And then when I ask them, what are you
doing when you are there? They say they have their phone there, they get calls, they look at their,
look at their emails. And then they are so worn out that they dropped down in front of the TV
set to watch the next soccer game. You know, well, look, I mean, that's not how you build relationships.
I mean, people want to be treated with respect. And one of the things is that compartmentalization,
to basically say, literally shut the thoughts of business out, out of your mind. And you can play
the same thing with your mind to say, look, I have these different doors, you know, where thoughts
belong to. And when your mind starts to bring up thoughts, you say they don't belong here at the
dinner table. It's much like you tell your assistant to say, you know, or your whole team,
you can call me anytime, literally anytime, if there's something that is risking the safety
of the team or sinking our business. But if it's not passing this criteria, you know,
tonight, you know, I have a meeting with my, my future wife tonight, I am out for dinner, you know,
and, and if you have a situation like this, call me, please call me. But if it's not in that
category, just send me a short text. And when I have time, I call back. I think people will
understand that. And it greatly helps running, running a good business and running your life
well. So it's a lot about setting the right expectations. That's also right. I mean, you have to
ideally make these things very clear to your team. And hopefully they learn from it because it helps
everybody. But do you have any specific rules that you follow when it comes to these different
situations? Well, I just mentioned the one to you. I mean, if it's not, if it's not a safety
issue or sink, sink the ship, you know, I have certain times lots where I won't, I won't want to have
cause. One other thing is one of the best advice I got was from a long time friend who told me
class, you're now going into executive roles. So make sure at the beginning of the year that you
schedule your vacations. And, and I thought, oh, what an odd, what an odd advice is that? But then I
realized over the years, the way this works is you, if you don't have the slot, you know, then
your office fills it and you yourself fill it. And then when you're thinking, oh my god, but when
am I going to spend some time, you know, when I, you have no, no slot left. So it's better to basically
put the slots in and then nibble on the ends of the slots. I'll give one up, give one up and say,
this is more important. I want to do this. You know, I want to build this relationship. But if you
don't put it into your calendar, you know, the likelihood that you, you will be very miserable as
supine. Something that we're talking about now, but it's often used with another term is work
life balance. What's your view on works role in life? I always thought that it is a wrong way
to frame it because I always thought work is a part of my life. If I, if I, if I'd, and the unfortunate
thing is that many people feel so miserable about their work that they don't ever want it to be a
part of their life. And that's when my other mantra comes in, love it, change it, or leave it,
right? Because the time spent in your, in your, in your business is going to be, it's going to be
long. And I think the one wake up call that I would give as a shout out versus, and I also
cover this in my book, what you can learn from the dying. There's not not that much research,
but there's one wonderful research done on, on what do people say on their deathbed, right? And,
and the, the, the most important things that people say on their deathbed are things like,
I wish I had allowed myself to be more happy, right? I wish I had not listened to others as much
and be more myself, right? There's no one, not one single person that I wish I had spent more
time in the business, right? And, and, and again, I think that this, that dichotomy between business
and, and life is a, is an industrial concept. And, and I, we're not living in an industrial world
anymore. We're living in a post-industrial world. And it's blended much, much more. So my
recommendation is, let's, let's use the same rigorous standard, how you evaluate your business
than other aspects of your life. Don't see it as that's my, that's my drag, and I need that money
because it's not true. I mean, you can find other ways. You know, by the way, there's another aspect
in there, which I always see as this aspect of fear. But people say, Oh, you know, Claus, you can
say that, you know, because now you are financially independent, but I did the same things when I had
nothing, right? And I think what, what happened is that I somehow found a way to deal with fear,
you know, in a way it was, I was forced to do something, you know, that, that was it. But I
call fear the false expectation appearing real, right? So, so because very often it is in our mind,
what do we make of it? What do we think is going to happen? And when we truly reflect on when
have we overcome fear and what then really happened, it's very often, it's a process on the positive
and very rarely it's a process on the negative. So let's shift focus to what you call the
outer game, which is the second part of the book. What is the outer game? The outer game is basically,
I mean, in my look, it's a targeted towards leaders, you know, so the outer game focuses mainly on
classic leadership issues, whereas the inner game is really more about your own operating system,
which you bring to the business world and to the private world, which we just talked about, you know?
So I cover those aspects that I consider are most important to build and run a business. I'm
starting from how do you evaluate whether a business is going to be an attractive business,
and how do you evaluate whether this, what offers you can do to have sustainable competitive
advantages? How does that work? So relatively simple things, but unfortunately, not that often
well understood, you know? And then it goes to my strong belief is the only sustainable
competitive advantage, long-term that you have in today's fast-changing world is people, the
talent that you bring to the place and how they work together. And also, then the question is,
oh, well, how do you, what is talent? How do you assess talent and how do you recruit talent so
that you are attractive to then develop them? And how do you make people work together? How do you
build high-performance teams? So those are aspects in there. And the other question is, what's my
own leadership style? You know, the endless discussion is it better to lead with fear or with love?
You know, and this is not it, not that simple an answer. Happy to talk about that more, you know,
but by the way, I just covered it this week in my LinkedIn, in my LinkedIn post, you know,
of anybody wants to read a little bit more about it. And so, yeah, so those type of things are
those type of things are in there. And then the question is, how do I motivate people, you know,
also to do the right things, as well as to do the things right? All of the classic, the classic,
more classic business things. I covered a little bit about your background in the introduction,
but I think this is a fitting place to speak a little bit more about your experiences and your
how you became a leader for two Fortune 500 companies. So, I started from not exactly the bottom,
but also not from the top. I started relatively low, and I already mentioned in the beginning,
what was my main motivation. I didn't come with the idea of, hey, you know, one day I will run
the Siemens or Alcoa. Alcoa was a different bargain because I basically was hired to be the CEO.
But at Siemens, I worked my way up, and there were plenty of moments where I thought that I should
probably leave the organization. And then interestingly, the organization realized probably that
that was going on in my mind and gave me bigger things to chew on and also promoted me.
I think sometimes it was the unsolvable problems that were thrown at a young kid and then somehow
we solved it. And I say, we, because one of the great things that I appreciate, I was always able
to redefine enormous talent inside of the organization or attract them to the organization and
build high performance teams. I'm an addict to building high performance teams and was with this
able to do things that alone I would have never been able to achieve. And then word spreads around
and one day you are considered to run the whole thing. But in between many, many challenges,
many, many challenges, many, many cultural situations that you get tested on. Because it was 20 years
with Siemens, you know. So this long time, long time. Definitely. And how was that transition
then into Alcoa? Well, different because when I became the CEO of Siemens, I knew the company
very, very well. I extremely well, because I worked in many, many different business areas. So,
so I had an idea on what I felt was needed and what the levers were for this. At Alcoa,
I was on the board of Alcoa, but only for a few years before. So I had an idea about the company
but it never worked inside. So I became, I came clearly as hired to become the CEO, the previous one
wanted out to do other things in life. And so I took over. So the approach was different in many
ways because I also started a listening tour inside of Alcoa to acquaint myself with the customers
as well as as well as with the employees and allowed myself a little time to dive deeper.
The fascinating thing that I learned from this is even though I consider myself a very active
board member, how little I really knew about what really needed to be done, right? And I think
this led to the reflection because on what's the role of boards? Because I've seen on boards
sometimes, this tends you to say, hey, let's get in, let's roll this leaf up and we can do it better
in a way. I would be extremely careful with this. If the board thinks that they can run the operations,
I think that's a misunderstanding, sometimes very expensive misunderstanding of what the role of the
board is. The role of the board is the most important, one of the most important roles of the
board is to find the right person to run it. So if you feel that it's not well run, then hell,
I mean, find somebody else to run it, right? That is the most important thing and that's what they
should focus on as one aspect. Then there are a few other things. Yeah, I think it's really interesting
that you include a chapter on board of directors and you have been on both sides, but from a CEO
perspective, how is it to have a board as your boss? Yeah, there's one of the most intense changes
between being in a normal leadership position and being the CEO. And I think most of the CEOs
want to realize that when they are in it, because what happens is when you move through the ranks,
you have always have bosses, but you have one person. So you know the person, you know what are
the trigger points of this individual, what are the priorities. So it's relatively easy to build a
